rv.q: Burnout Paradise is exceptionally brief -- it ran less than my travel time to and from St. Ann's -- yet it is wildly original and consistently riotous, the company applying itself to its nonsensical goals with total conviction.
It’s the most fun you’re likely to have with experimental theater this season.
For 65 minutes their “near burnout” is pure entertainment for the rest of us.
Pony Cam ultimately undercuts their collective’s originality with an unnecessary post-script performance, but still, Burnout Paradise is one of the best nights out this fall.
Perhaps the best thing about Burnout Paradise is the way it makes a collective of its entire audience.

In the end, the combination of the absurd with the high level of audience participation feels less like a performance (and they, less like performers), and more like neighbors in a truly unique and communal theatrical experience.

cn.t: Australian collective Pony Cam's audacious experiment literalizes modern burnout with performers tackling everyday tasks on treadmills in this "maddest entertainment in town"—critics praise the committed chaos and clever metaphor.
